title.rendered: Ifeyinwa Arinze Won A Locarno Residency. It’s Only the Beginning

content.rendered:
Ify Arinze had no plan to go into filmmaking. At least initially. Born to a dad who passed on early and a mum who worked in immigration, she left Lagos for the US in 2010, planning to study biochemistry—“just like Ben Carson”—and on to med school. Her plan was similar to the plans of many immigrants before her: she wanted to “make my family proud”.

Somehow, she discovered neuroscience and decided to study it at a college for women. That became her first degree not biochemistry. Outside of class, she discovered photography and got good enough to get gigs to cover weddings. When she graduated, she took up a job at the University of Massachusetts and then moved to Michigan. At this point, medicine remained in her future but again, something else intervened: she wanted to go to film school. Unlike the move biochemistry to neuroscience, the move to film had to be trickier, so she spoke to a few people in her orbit who had made the tranistion. These were mainly engineers. Subsequently, she found out that she needed to submit a video sample as part of her application. 

Arinze arranged a ragtag crew of friends to make a short film. “It was very DIY,” she says over Google Meet. “YouTube was my teacher.”

The result of that hustle was “Cooking with My Mum”, the story of a girl who has forgotten how to cook jollof rice and has to reach out to her mum for help ahead of hosting a party at her new home. The first-time director loved the experience and decided to do another short. She put both films in her applications to five schools, NYU and Columbia in Chicago among them. “I didn’t have too high expectations,” she says. “I was just proud of myself of having done it.”

Well, low expectations be damned. She got offers from both Columbia and NYU. “It felt like validation,” she says. “Sometimes you think ‘I’m just following my instincts’ and then you get this external affirmation.” 

She chose NYU. The school had offered a substantial scholarship but, she adds, it still was stressful to come with the rest of the cash for her education. She eventually spent five years instead of the official three years, mostly because of the pandemic. This wasn’t a problem. “You don’t pay tuition for the last two years and you are making work while you are in the programme,” she says.

At NYU, she met Spike Lee; he’s the artistic director of the programme. She also met Casey Lemmons, Alex Rockwell, Chloe Zhao, and Charlotte Wells. I ask her if Nollywood came up while she was there and she says not really. But Chuko Esiri, half of the Esiri Brothers, the pair behind the acclaimed Eymiofe, came up a few times. He is an NYU grad. When Nollywood did come up, it was because of her nationality. How familiar is Arinze herself with the industry? Quite familiar, she says, although that’s because of childhood sessions with her grandmother. 

“We would always watch films together,” she says, laughing at the memory. “Ini Edo was her favourite.” 

***

One of Arinze’s popular shorts is Breastmilk. It was her thesis film and was based on a short story by her friend Pemi Aguda. “It felt so vivid that I thought ‘I’d love to make this into a film’.” She got Aguda’s permission and returned to Nigeria to shoot it. She had wanted to be on set for five days shooting Breastmilk but saw that her crew members, already used to Nigerian productions, said they should be done in one day. Even now, Arinze seems amused, if mildly aghast, at the idea. “We are not making that type of film,” she told them. A negotiation followed and finally she was on set for four days. 

That was years ago. Arinze has since written a feature, which took her to a filmmaking programme in Mexico, to the Berlinale Talents’ Script Station, and to the Locarno Residency. The feature project is currently titled Scruples, and the idea came after a conversation with Aguda in which they mulled the absence of proper boarding school films set in Nigeria. Aguda, who seems like Arinze’s muse, suggested that Arinze writes such a film. The resulting story, a “vomit draft” as she calls it, is based on memories and experiences of her time as a pupil in Queens’ College, Lagos. “The story didn’t have much shape, so my work over the past five years has been finding the shape and structure, and also [to give it] a beginning, middle, and end.”

The story covers the power and class dynamics at a girls’ secondary school through the eyes of a student who becomes enamoured of the institution’s head girl. She becomes a “less ethical version of herself” until the near-death experience of a close friend forces a reckoning. I tell Arinze that the synopsis shared by Locarno hinted at a queer relationship between the girls at the centre of the story. Arinze shrugs and says she doesn’t think Scruples is “explicitly queer”. “There’s a fine line between liking somebody so much that you can’t tell if you want to be them or be with them,” she adds. 

What is certain is the film would explore class differences between two girls at a secondary school in Nigeria.

For Arinze, those three days in Switzerland were a “whirlwind”. She pitched on one day, had meetings with the Locarno jury on the second, and then, on the last day, she attended an event where three winning projects were announced. Arinze was winner of the grand prize. The win came with a cash prize of CHF5,000, a yearlong script mentorship, a trip to Venice, another to the south of France, and finally a trip back to Locarno for a presentation where she’d give a progress report. In the time it has taken this interview to be published, these activities must have come to an end. At the time she wasn’t sure when the film will be ready for the public but she gave 2027 as the year she intends to start shooting.

One reason for the length of time it will take is Arinze’s unhurried mode of working. Another is logistical. Given that the film involves kids in school, shooting has to be during a long vacation. In the meantime, Arinze says she’s seeking grants while working in New York, teaching high school students documentary filmmaking.  

***

Arinze is aware that she is emerging as a filmmaker in a season where Nigerian filmmakers are showing up at the biggest film stages. CJ Obasi showed Mami Wata in Sundance, Akinola Davies Jnr premiered My Father’s Shadow in Cannes, the Esiri brothers had Eyimofe in Berlin, and Damilola Orimogunje will screen his latest, Dear Ajayi, at one of the parallel sections of Venice. It’s a great time to be a Nigerian making movies targeting an international audience. Pressed a bit on where she would like to see Scruples premiere, she laughs somewhat nervously as though she doesn’t want any of her dream venues to get jealous. “You are putting me in a tough spot,” she says, pauses, and goes off the record.

“I want it to be celebrated and I want it to be seen,” she says finally, laughing at her reluctance to make her dreams public.

As the interview winds down, I ask Arinze if she thinks of herself as a Nollywood filmmaker. In response, she accuses me of asking a trick question. She says she was raised on a “Nollywood die” but she continues, “I think of myself as a Nigerian filmmaker because the way I like to make work may not be conducive to Nollywood based on the experience I had shooting Breastmilk and hearing how things are done. I move much slower.” I am not sure if she has answered the question so I ask how she feels about Nigeria’s mainstream in contemporary times. “You are trying to put me in trouble,” she says and doesn’t answer. 

She is, however, happy to name Djibril Diop Mambety and Sembene. For African filmmakers who are alive, she doesn’t name the directors but mentions two films: This Is Not A Burial, It Is A Resurrection and On Becoming A Guinea Fowl. 

Her models for execution are not any of those films. For her, the models are the works of Lucretia Martel and Hirokazu Kore-eda. “My voice as a filmmaker is a lot quieter,” she says. “It is not melodramatic—which is not to say that melodramatic things don’t have a place—but when I saw Hirokazu Koreada’s work I saw that the stakes are quite high but the tone is quieter and more poetic. That’s where my films tend to live: in the quiet, and in the poetic, and in the intimate.”

excerpt.rendered: Ify Arinze talks about winning the Locarno Residency in 2025, her life before filmmaking, and her plans for a feature film.

title.rendered: 4 Reasons Nollywood Is Years Away From A Truly Cool Epic

content.rendered:
Certain things are just cool. There’s no way to explain why they are cool they just are. In Nollywood, there are only a handful of cool people. This doesn’t diminish everyone else making good stuff that we praise and admire, but cool is its very own class.

Across directors, producers, and actors, there are only a few unobjectionable cool people who have graced our screens or still do in some way today: RMD, Genevieve, Rita Dominic, young Olu Jacobs, Pete Edochie at every age, Jim Iyke, and Omotola. Some less popular cool figures include Sango’s Wale Adebayo and Charles Okpaleke.

It’s a short list in my opinion, but cool people are few and far between. And so are cool movies.

***

In Hollywood, The Rock was cool, Chuck Norris was cool, Tom Cruise is cool. Even over 80, Arnold Schwarzenegger is cool.

There is no cooler genre of film than Epic and Fantasy. A great many otherwise subpar stories have become cultural stories, for example Conan the Barbarian, based on the rule of cool alone. Everything else be damned.

As Nollywood has continued to grow, our cinematography has gotten better and our storytelling has more or less become more structured, even if I can’t bring myself to say the stories are better. But we’ve not gotten cooler. Let’s look at a few examples of cool historical fantasy from elsewhere.

TROY

The bronze age costumes accurately represented, Eric Bana and Brad Pitt in the form of their lives, fight scenes, and quips that make no sense but stay with you regardless.

KINGDOM OF HEAVEN

Ed Norton’s masked King Baldwin. It has knights, it has armies, it has fire, it looked cool.

KING ARTHUR: LEGEND OF THE SWORD

Guy Ritchie looked at Ancient British mythology and was like, I need spice, flavour and a whole lot of my twist on this story and it looked cool.

MZANSI MAGIC’S SHAKA ILEMBE

The team behind this spared nothing to ensure that this project was visually titillating. From battle scenes, to command performances, there’s a rawness in it that somehow translated to cool. Maybe for me it was cool that someone on the continent has presented their own legend in a way that Nollywood has failed to.

So, Nollywood isn’t cool?

That would be the wrong thing to infer here because VCD-era Nollywood delivered coolness in spades. New Nollywood just hasn’t been able to do so. And for that to change, certain things need to happen.

A Return to Individual Expression: There will only ever be few persons who are capable of creating stories from a perspective outside of conventional expectations. We need to allow for directors who can elevate the scripts they are given. I’m not saying we need auteurs, but maybe we need more auteur-leaning directors, even if in Nollywood I see this more in early-career filmmakers. Maybe the industry as it is currently structured beats this trait out of its directors.

Did Pat Nebo Die with All The Good Costumes? A great component of cool shit is cool looks: the costumes, the locale, the backgrounds, the set dressings. In most Nollywood period projects, there’s been a focus on accuracy without a commensurate attention on coolness. Both are not mutually exclusive components. Until we find a way to bring in historically accurate components with cool aesthetics, we’re not making it out of the trenches of the bland and ordinary.

Budgets! I recall an experience where a writing team I was part of was told to axe certain scenes because the project’s budget would not be enough. However. budgets and their unique ability to never be enough for a project are not new concepts that apply only to Nollywood. But Nollywood producers’ inability to prioritise budgets for what matters and to squeeze through with just good enough art direction, set designs, and props because the right way is “too expensive” is why most Nollywood epics look dated and sickly a year or two after release.

We Can’t write Cool Shit? There are a lot of lines, words, and phrases that just take over the Zeitgeist. Solo Leveling has “Arise!” Jujutsu Kaisen has “Nah, I’d win”, and before then, Terminator had “I’ll be back”. Gerard Butler’s “This is Sparta!” became a thing and Shola Shobowale gave us “Welcome to a new dispensation”.

Cool writing is wish-fulfilment contained within the sandbox of competent writing. Plot holes can be forgiven if a fantastical, and charismatic character gets to win the day in cool fashion, says a quippy or really insightful remark and rides off into the sunset.

There’s a lack of one liners, catchy stuff, cool sounding lines that have come out of Nigerian cinema in the last decade. Is it that, somehow, Nollywood is both pervasive and simultaneously out of the Zeitgeist? Or do we not have moments in scripts that culminate into a quotable moment of glorious aura farming? Or is it that marketing for our projects is absolute dog water that we do not know how to capitalise on what we have?

I think the answer lies outside of the industry itself. It lies in economics. Every film ecosystem in recent times that has “come out of nowhere” to create something cool or relevant has been directly tied to a period of economic boom or financial transition that upends the current systems that finances only a certain type of film or project according to previously established conventions—conventions that would have prevented aspiring filmmakers with a different vision or aesthetic from creating something cool. China is a good example. As its economy has grown, it has been able to make Nezha 2 and have it be the highest grossing animated movie ever, as well as countless other forays across television and gaming (see Black Myth Wukong or The Legend of Hei).

I think Nollywood missed its moment. In the late aughts, cinemas had become a thing again; audiences were primed, both mentally and economically for a resurgent Nollywood and the country waited with bated breath. What, for example, would Igodo but made for the big screen, with the right budget have looked like? So maybe it’s not economics alone. It’s the lack of a collective desire to do cool shit. Nollywood needs to create something that stands as a beacon of the industry, the first frame of reference for anyone when they talk about Nollywood in the future. But I don’t know that we have reached the point where the industry’s collective consciousness is aligned towards that ambition.

excerpt.rendered: Why Nollywood cinema needs to make cool shit to capture the world’s attention.

title.rendered: Will Niava’s Wonderful Journey From Ghana to Canada to 2026 Sundance Triumph

content.rendered:
Few weeks after his own American success, Will Niava is speaking about the last couple of filmmakers from the continent to have shown their film and won awards at the world’s biggest independent film festival. Naturally, he seems joyful. Was he aware that, a couple years before, another West African filmmaker had won the same award he took at the prestigious festival? He is and he mentions the name—Akinola Davies Jnr—immediately. “The fact that he won meant that my voice could also be heard around the world,” he says. “You can see the things that it has done for his career and these are the things that I am looking for.”

He then goes on to mention other African filmmakers who have been to Utah for Sundance before the internet temporarily freezes up his image on my screen. He is, obviously, a student of Africa’s success at international venues. Which is a good thing because he is now one of those success stories.

Although based in Canada, Niava is speaking from Accra, where his mother, a Ghanaian, lives and where he was raised from age 12 after his birth, in Abidjan, to two high-profile linguists. He talks about his dad, an Ivorian, translating for Mandela and his mum doing work for the WHO, his respect for both of them about as audible in his voice as his cosmopolitanism. His Sundance-winning short, Jazz Infernal, is dedicated to the memory of his father.

Niava is himself a dad now—a “hands-on parent”, as he calls it—to an 8-month-old baby. Which tells me he’s riding quite the high: Bicoastal living, new baby, Sundance award. It’s a charmed life.

In fact, to get, perhaps, a hint of a setback for the reigning champion of international Sundance short films, you might have to go back—way back.

***

As a kid, he had been a big fan of football and might have gone on to be a professional player but there was one quirk: he was classmates with Jordan Ayew, future captain of the Ghanaian senior football team. As young men, both were students of Lycée Français International Jacques Prévert d’Accra, which he says is Accra’s only school accredited by French authorities. Ayew was so good on the football field that Niava had to reconsider his ambitions.

“His older brother, Andre Ayew, was two classes ahead,” he says. “And after a while, we realised that if there’s anyone who’s going to be a footballer in this school, it’s these two guys. Jordan was always more skilful and Andre had the drive. These guys wake up at 4am to go to the field… I don’t have that level of dedication to football. So, what’s it that I like?”

He had interests in camera and had been in a few plays. But the thing would arrive fully when he was admitted to an American school in Ghana, which his parents chose because they wanted him to go to the US for college. It was in this school that Niava’s dream of filmmaking was kindled; around the same time, he became friendly with someone doing stop motion.

Somehow, his parents changed their minds about the US when it was time, likely because of the spectre of American violence, especially against black men. Why not Canada? His two sisters were already living there. Niava didn’t think this was a great option. For obvious reasons: Which college-aged teenager wants to live with his sister?

An application to NAFTI, Ghana’s main film school, had already fallen through by then because the school felt he didn’t need them. “They said I was doing things they hadn’t been taught.”

Wasn’t this about as flattering as any rejection could be?

Not immediately, he says. A rejection is a rejection. His dad thought otherwise; he had encouraged his kid to do whatever he wanted and that rejection suggested he was on to something. “My parents were one of kind for African parents,” he says.  

It was that rejection by NAFTI that spurred two applications to Canadian schools: one in Ottawa and another in Montreal. He chose to apply to just two because he didn’t want “to be rejected by a lot of people”. He had no need to worry. Both said yes, and he chose Montreal partly because he didn’t have a sister in the city. That the city was also French-speaking was appealing to this bilingual kid.

At Montreal, he found their French weird and tried to sign up for the directing class in school but it was filled: “there were only 10 spots”. He got into the documentary class, which he now believes was a blessing. “It taught me how to capture life without a script,” he says, adding that he likes to work with non-actors.

He was there for two years, and when he came out in 2010, he took to directing music videos. There might be other older videos of his lurking on the internet but he says with a laugh that he’d rather they remain anonymous.

***

Not very long after, Niava had an idea that one of his music video projects could be a short film. One reason he had this thought was that he was on set for a short film titled Fauve, which was directed by his pal Jeremy Comte. “I know I can do this too,” he thought to himself. It probably helped his conviction that Fauve received an Oscar nomination in 2019.

So, he wrote a film script his next music video clients loved. The budget was 5000 dollars. Somehow, a friend from LA who was about to start a production outfit read the script and pledged 10,000 dollars. This meant they had 15,000 dollars for the short. “I had never heard this type of money in my life,” he says.

Titled Zoo, this short, which he says was edited in haste, was the first time he was on a set like that one. Naturally, he wasn’t too sure what was happening. Still, he managed to pull it off using “the confidence I had seen on Jeremy’s set to almost fake it.”

Zoo got to the people at Sundance but they weren’t interested. “I remember them bouncing me,” he says. But there was enough in the material for another edit, which Comte suggested. Subsequently, another version was cut and prepared. But the team couldn’t find a distributor. “They said, ‘Your film doesn’t represent our values; it feels a little too Americanised and honestly it’s not a great take on what happens in Quebec.’”

So, the crew decides to figure out how to distribute their film. And then something tragic happened in the US that had rather positive repercussions for Niava and company: the George Floyd video goes viral. “It’s crazy because the way he gets killed is similar to what happened in my film … and without warning, there is this wave of emails.”

Suddenly, this short film that couldn’t find distribution gets invited to scores of festivals, winning awards in the process. “We ended up keeping all the money that we got from the film and didn’t share it with any distributor.”

One of the festivals the film got invited to was Clermont Ferrand, the famous short film festival. There, he met Ghanaian director Anthony Nti, who won the festival’s big prize for Da Yie. “It’s like we were all getting the light at that moment.”

His winning streak continued with a call from Criterion. “It was the most validating thing. I was like wait, ‘This is my first film!’”  

He sounds incredulous even now.

***

In February this year, Paradise, a film written by Niava and Comte was screened at the Berlin Film Festival. Set in Ghana and in English, French, and Twi, Paradise got Niava into the sights of Canadian funding bodies, like SODEC, and this came in handy when he was ready with a project of his own.

That project was inspired by a conversation he had with Ange-Eric N’guessan, a Montreal-based musician famous in Ivory Coast but pretty much unknown in Canada. After what sounds like a hilarious exchange, Niava thought they could make a film out of their experiences on their first day in the city they now call home.

A first screenplay didn’t work, its main feedback coming from his Trinidadian-Sri Lankan wife. She told him that since he wasn’t going to therapy or even speaking to her or crying about the loss of his father, maybe he could put all of that pent-up grief in his art. “It hurt my ego but it was coming out of love and care,” he says.

If you have seen the Jazz Infernal, you know that he did exactly what his wife told him. The film is not just dedicated to Niava’s dad, the loss of a father is cleft into the fabric of the narrative. N’guessan plays the lead role as a man who finds himself in Canada and meets two men who recognise his last name and take him to a club where they say his father once played. From that point on, chaotic things happen to our hero.

As you might expect from a former music video director, the film is charged with sound and movement. The technical aspects of the film—the editing, lighting, and cinematography—are flawless. “I wanted it to have my touch, that fast-paced style. I wanted it to feel like free jazz. I wanted it to feel like a Fela Kuti song. That’s the intention I went in with.”

The film’s remarkable editing was carried out by Niava himself and two other persons, one of which is Thomas Bellefleur, an editor who had worked on the 2022 Oscar nominated short film Invincible.

TIFF was the first big festival to accept Jazz Infernal. It opened the festival and Niava seemed to have big hopes that it would win the festival’s main award for its category. It didn’t; the winner was an animation picture that ended up Canada’s submission for the 2026 Oscars. When it got picked for the Oscars, Niava admitted the rival picture was deserving, and over the video call, he appeared to retain the sportsmanship that he probably had all those years ago as a footballer-manque. While, he is competitive, he’s also able to accept a fair loss.

In any case, a win was on the way.

***

Anyone familiar with the workings of the Big 5 film festivals knows that they love a world premiere, which makes it pretty difficult to see that any two festivals on that list accepting the same project. Jazz Infernal became one of the few films to sway programmers at both festivals. “Sundance got over 11,000 submissions, chose 54, and Jazz Infernal was the only one that had previously screened in Toronto,” he says.

When Niava attended screenings at Sundance, he was mesmerised by some of the other projects the festival had selected. He mentions his admiration of Birdie, an impressive short film made by Praise Odigie Paige, a Nigerian-American filmmaker. In fact, as he tells it, he felt Paige’s film was going to be the winner. So, on the night, he decided to just enjoy the festival’s drink and food. So, when the awards were called out, he was far back at the venue in Park City. But then he won as Jazz Infernal received the Short Film Jury Award: International Fiction. Four years before, it was Davies Jnr. It was now his turn.

The win means Jazz Infernal might get a shot at the 2027 Oscars. So perhaps the right culture funding bodies in Canada will consider sponsoring a campaign. In the meantime, Niava says that the success of Davies Jnr’s Lizard and My Father’s Shadow and CJ Obasi’s Mami Wata leads him to believe that the world is ready for stories from Sub-Saharan Africa.

He is now working on a feature film he says will cost a few million dollars to pull off. Asked if that’s a lot, he laughs and says, “There are people who would consider that amount too much and those who would say it’s nothing. I am looking for the second group.”

He is unwilling to say anything specific about the film but he knows it will be ambitious. The man who was born in Ivory Coast, raised in Ghana, and now lives in Canada wants to shoot a film that would involve China and in Ghana. “It’s something that is going to stir a lot of people,” he says. He agrees that such an outline is controversial but adds that controversy is merely a byproduct of his intentions.

“I just want to raise a mirror to ourselves,” he says, “[so we] see what we are doing to our earth and see what we are doing to our people.”

excerpt.rendered: The Sundance award-winner speaks about his life from Abidjan to Accra to Montreal.

title.rendered: AMVCA 2026: 5 Lessons From the Ceremony

content.rendered:
Over the weekend, we were at the 12th edition of the AMVCA 2026 ceremony at the Eko Hotel and Suites in Victoria Island, Lagos, Nigeria. While there, we learned a few things about the state of the Nigerian film industry. Five of those lessons are below.

5. Box-office success & excellence may not mix

Gingerrr, Behind the Scenes, and Oversabi Aunty, three of Nollywood’s highest grossing films ever, got multiple nominations but altogether scored 0 wins.

So perhaps the AMVCA is learning a lesson that commercial viability is not a substitute for artistic
coherence and excellence. Does this mean Nollywood is entering a phase where its institutions understand the difference between popularity and quality? We hope so. 

4. Maybe coproductions need own categories

One of the main themes of the night was My Father’s Shadow overshadowing The Herd. This felt a little unfair given the difference in budgets and the privileges the former had courtesy of its coproduction status. Maybe a distinct category needs to be created?

3. Canal+ needs the AMVCA as diplomacy

The AMVCA is more than an awards platform. The awards are one of the few places where every faction of the industry still gathers under a single umbrella: mainstream filmmakers, veterans, streaming players, actors, marketers and television executives. For Canal+, friendliness to the entire ecosystem is strategic. It’s a French company but it needs to keep the influential English film industry on its side. 

2. Speed is not always a virtue at award shows

The show was boring after the first half-hour and before the last half-hour. And first-time host Bovi was not the problem. That blame should go to the structure of the show. The lull occured mostly when Bovi was off-stage.

What was the issue? The stretch of time with only awards presentations didn’t quite work, even if it ostensibly was done like so to speed things up. It needed Bovi to inject some energy, some rhythm
but he was missing. This means that IK Osakioduwa remains the exemplar host at the AMVCA. 

1. Being undeniable is the most powerful
campaign strategy

Bucci Franklin’s turn as Oboz in To Kill A Monkey was the only assured win before the ceremony. And when he was named winner of the Best Supporting Actor category, it was the loudest
cheer of the night. It is not always the case that great performances find massive popularity. But it happened this time.

excerpt.rendered: 12th edition of the AMVCA threw up some surprises but one win was always certain.

title.rendered: Cannes 2026: Ghana’s Ama Ampadu Announced As Critics’ Week Juror

content.rendered:
Ghanaian-British producer Ama Ampadu is among a group of 4 jurors announced by the Semaine de la Critique section of Cannes.

The group will be led by Payal Kapadia, the Indian filmmaker who was named winner of Cannes’ Grand Prix award at the festival in 2024. Others on the jury include actor Théodore Pellerin, singer-songwriter Oklou, and journalist Donsaron Kovitvanitcha.

This year, the Critics’ Week section has chosen a single film from the continent, “What Do the Maknines Dream”, a 23-minute short from Franco-Algerian filmmaker Sarra Ryma.

Ampadu has enjoyed a storied career in the film industry, becoming an executive at the BFI Film Fund in 2023. She has also had a longstanding relationship with Cannes. Back in 2015, she produced Lamb, which became the first film from Ethiopia to be showcased at the prestigious film festival. And last year, three films from the BFI appeared at Cannes, including My Father’s Shadow, which was Nigeria’s first film in competition at the popular French film festival.

Ampadu grew up in North London and has previously worked at the United Nations. She was credited as an associate producer on Mati Diop’s Dahomey.

excerpt.rendered: Ampadu’s Critics’ Week jury at Cannes will be led by Indian director Payal Kapadia.

title.rendered: Senegal’s Angèle Diabang Named To 2026 Cannes Un Certain Regard Jury

content.rendered:
Cannes’ 2026 Un Certain Regard jury will include the Senegalese producer and director Angele Diabang. She will be joined by Italian director Laura Samani, Lebanon composer Khaled Mouzanar, and French director Thomas Cailley in a jury led by French actress Leïla Bekhti as President.

Last year, Diabang was responsible for bringing an adaptation of Mariama Bâ’s popular novel So Long a Letter to the big screen. The film was screened at the Locarno Film Festival in Switzerland among other venues. In 2019, her short A Tune of Kora won an award at FESPACO.

In a bio published on the Cannes website, the festival highlights her work on documentaries, stating that the filmmaker “has been developing a body of work focused on social issues, women’s journeys, and human rights through her production company Karoninka, founded in 2006”.

As part of her work on the jury, Diabang will assess the merit of the 15 films announced by the festival’s director, Thierry Fremaux. Those 15 projects include 3 films from African filmmakers: Rafiki Fariala from the Congo, Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo from Rwanda, and Morocco’s Laïla Marrakchi.

Speaking about her role as jury president, Bekhti said, “Working in cinema has taught me that movies are places of encounter with others, with oneself, with the world. Discovering them alongside a jury, living this timeless experience, is both a responsibility and a joy. I look forward to the exchanged perspectives, the dialogues, and the doubts as well, which make up the richness of this living art”.

excerpt.rendered: Diabang will join a jury led by French actress Leïla Bekhti.

title.rendered: Lagos State Government Partners “Uncredited” Screenwriting Project

content.rendered:
The Lagos State Government has partnered with Uncredited Africa, a screenwriting programme launched by Lani Aisida. The partnership would be carried out by two bodies under the government: the Office of Political, Legislative and Civic Engagement as well as the Ministry of Wealth Creation and Employment.

According to a statement by Uncredited Africa, the alliance is “a significant step toward building a sustainable creative economy by equipping emerging writers with the tools, access, and industry pathways needed to thrive professionally”.

Speaking about the development, Aisida said the programme will do more than teach screenwriting. It’s also about “building sustainable careers,” he said. “This partnership with Lagos State is a major step in creating an ecosystem where talented writers are not only trained but also connected to real opportunities to earn, grow, and thrive within the industry.”

Uncredited Africa’s screenwriting project is intended to produce screenplays ready for production. The project will also involve pitch sessions to producers.  

“This partnership reflects our continued commitment to engaging young people in meaningful and productive ventures,” said Sholabomi Shasore, who serves as Permanent Secretary at the Office of Political, Legislative and Civic Engagement. “Storytelling is a powerful civic tool, and through initiatives like Uncredited Africa, we are not only amplifying voices but also fostering a generation that can shape narratives, influence culture, and contribute to society in impactful ways.”

Ololade Aina, Shasore’s counterpart at the Ministry of Wealth Creation and Employment, said, “The creative industry holds immense potential for job creation and economic growth in Lagos State. By supporting Uncredited Africa, we are investing in a structured pathway that transforms raw talent into employable skills and viable careers.”  

The programme will take place across an 8-week period. See here for more details.

excerpt.rendered: The Uncredited Africa project will involve the production of market-ready screenplays.

title.rendered: Cannes 2026: Arie and Chuko Esiri Get Directors’ Fortnight Premiere For Virginia Woolf Adaptation Clarissa

content.rendered:
Following their appearance at the 2020 Berlin Film Festival, the Nigerian brothers Arie and Chuko Esiri will showcase their newest film, Clarissa, at the Cannes Film Festival sidebar Directors’ Fortnight.

According to the organisers of the sidebar, the coming edition will feature projects “from 19 countries on five continents, with notable contributions from a number of countries with little or no international exposure, such as Nigeria, Sudan, Guatemala, Venezuela and Cyprus”. Notably, the brothers are the only African filmmakers with feature projects in the sidebar.

Clarissa is an adaptation of the Virginia Woolf 1925 novel, Mrs Dalloway, and it stars Sophie Okonedo, David Oyelowo, Ayo Edebiri and Nikki Amuka-Bird. In December 2025, it was announced that famed firm NEON had acquired its distribution. A revered novel from the acclaimed British writer, Mrs Dalloway entered the public domain in 2021.

The 2026 Cannes Film Festival runs from May 12th until May 23rd.

excerpt.rendered: Nigeria has secured back-to-back representation at Cannes for the first time in its history.

title.rendered: Cannes 2026: Three African Filmmakers Invited to Directors’ Fortnight

content.rendered:
Three projects from Africa have been selected by the Cannes sidebar Directors’ Fortnight. While the sole feature from the continent is Clarissa by the Esiri brothers, two other projects have been programmed in the short and medium-length segment of the sidebar.

Sudanese director Ibrahim Omar will screen his fiction project Nothing Happens After Your Absence. This project follows his 2024 film, Nothing Happens After That. Also playing in the section is In Search of the Grey Bird with Green Stripes, a short documentary from Moroccan-French director Saïd Hamich Benlarbi. Benlarbi’s 2024 film, Across the Sea, received a special screening in the Critics’ Week section two years ago.

According to the organisers, the coming edition of the Directors’ Fortnight will feature projects “from 19 countries on five continents, with notable contributions from a number of countries with little or no international exposure, such as Nigeria, Sudan, Guatemala, Venezuela and Cyprus”.

The 2026 Cannes Film Festival runs from May 12th until May 23rd.

excerpt.rendered: Sudan, Morocco, and NIgeria are heading to Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight

title.rendered: Cannes 2026 To Welcome 3 African Filmmakers

content.rendered:
Ben’imana by Rwanda’s Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo, Congo Boy by Congo’s Rafiki Fariala and La Más Dulce (Strawberries) from French-Moroccan director Laïla Marrakchi are heading to the Cannes Film Festival according to a list released by the festival earlier today.

All three films will be screened in the Un Certain Regard section, which is usually reserved for newcomer filmmakers.

On the list, however, Dusabejambo is the sole debut filmmaker, the others having released projects over the years, including Fariala’s Nous Etudiants (We Students), which showed at the Berlin Film Festival in 2022. Marrakchi appeared in Cannes back in 2005 with her first feature Marock. Her second, Rock the Casbah, premiered at the 2013 Toronto International Film Festival.

excerpt.rendered: Three African filmmakers will screen projects at Cannes 2026 Un Certain Regard section.

title.rendered: Praise Odigie Paige’s (Very) Unusual Route To Sundance

content.rendered:
It is probably hyperbole to say that nobody has ever gotten to their first Sundance screening in the way that Praise Odigie Paige has. But it might be true.

A few years ago, she was an undocumented person in the US. Go back some years and she was a 10-year-old kid who had just moved to the US. Go even further and you’d find a kid growing up in Ibadan, Nigeria, raised by Esan parents in a family where nobody would have known that this child would be showing Birdie, an impressive short film about two immigrant daughters and a stranger from home, to a crowd of filmgoers at the 2026 edition of the Sundance Film Festival.

The day we speak, she is a figure on a screen with bright eyes and full, wild hair. The “writer-artist-filmmaker”, as she describes herself, is about as bubbly as her film is restrained, a gorgeous tightly written picture she wrote and directed herself. By way of a bio, she says she enters every story through “the lens of poetry even though I don’t write poems” and then says she had been living “precariously until recently”. This is how her previous status as undocumented gets into the conversation.

Obviously too young to understand what was happening at the time, Odigie Paige recalls her family receiving a letter with an ultimatum: they had 30 days to leave the US. “Clearly, we did not leave,” she laughs.

But even without grasping what exactly the problem was, she grew up with a sense of dread, which then became a feeling of being caged, given the impossibility of travel for the undocumented. She tells me that in recent years, she has had dreams where she’s hustling to go back to Nigeria in a manner similar to the harried manner her parents left their home country. (Somehow, her folks had missed their flight and were then given five minutes to get on the plane that eventually took them to the US.)

The Immigrant

In the US, Odigie Paige was going to become a popular immigrant cliché: she would study medicine and become a doctor. That changed when an aunt visiting from Nigeria expressed surprise at her course of study. Her aunt’s admonition didn’t immediately change her path, but when that aunt passed on sometime around 2011, she realised that “time can be wasted” and decided to give her love for storytelling a chance. This, assures me, is an abridged version of a much longer story. “There was so much pressure being the first of my family to go to college here, I felt I needed to do something ’serious’ with it but I just made a decision to do what I was born to do and that was film.”

Her complex journey links the emotional stakes of her Sundance short to her life. Birdie, she says, is seeking an answer to the question, “What does it feel to be separated from home…especially as a child?”

In writing the story, though, she was drawn to Nigeria’s history. It is why the film is set in the late sixties, during the Biafran War. But there is more to the story; in addition to the wartime immigrant perspective, there is also a sexual awakening of sorts for the film’s central character and what that experience does to the relationship between two sisters and between mother and daughter.

“The film is about your adolescence unfolding in the shadows of these adult catastrophes that no one really explains to you,” she says, adding that even as many things were happening when her family landed in the US, she most clearly recalls the feelings she and her sister had as they grew into their bodies.

“I am drawn to how displacement presses into private lives,” she says. “And things like shame and desire were a big part of my coming-of-age experience. But Birdie is also about a mother figuring out what it means to be unprepared in a time she can’t control.”

***

In the short film, the title appears to be a shortened version of Bernadette, the name of the film’s elder daughter (Precious Maduanusi). But there’s another reason it is titled so. “These are teenagers who just want to be free.”

Odigie Paige makes no real attempt to hide how much of her life is in the film, so I ask which of the film’s two girls represents her youth. It should be easy enough to say it is the one who gives the film its title and whose behaviour propels the plot but there’s a crease in that theory. Birdie’s story is narrated by her younger sister (Eniola Abioro), a Nick Carraway figure whose name is unsaid in the film.

“When I started the film, it was more from Birdie’s perspective,” she says, “but as people started to ask me about the story, I realised I wasn’t the sister who was making all these bold and risky choices. I was the one who was very mousy, who was obsessed with validation of my parents. I was the one standing in the doorway and trying to keep my sister in line.”

Shooting Birdie

The film was shot in Virginia in late 2024 during the American elections. “Appalachia,” she says. “Very rural.” To get her actresses, she went to different sources. She discovered Maduanusi on a casting website called Backstage. She wasn’t sure what character she’d play but she knew she wanted her for a role. She found Abioro on Instagram. Sheila Chukwulozie who plays mother to the daughters was found in a short film titled Egungun. Coincidentally, that film’s director, Olive Nwosu, showed her debut feature, Lady, at Sundance this year.

While Chukwulozie and Maduanusi are Igbo, Abioro is Yoruba. Odigie Praise is herself fully Esan—her mum is from Uromi; dad is from Iruekpen. She got married in 2019 and turned her original last name to her middle name. “I am the first born,” she says. “That name has to live on.”

Given the sensitivity of some Nigerians to matters concerning ethnicity, did she consider telling a story directly connected to the Biafra War a problem? She says she thought about it and decided that her “writing came from an honest place” and it was rooted in her own “personal experience”. It also helped that she grew up with in an environment with a lot of Igbo people. She adds that she partnered with the right people so when they said they felt “seen, that was enough validation that I was telling the story correctly”.

There’s no stopping her now. There’s a feature film also involving Biafra in her future. She tells me that Nigeria’s main war is a “story that needs to be told and be told in a specific way”. To tell it, she would “focus on the emotional cost of war on women—young women, older women”.

***

Birdie’s cinematography, one of its highlights, was commandeered by Lidia Nikonova, with whom she was to work with on a previous project that didn’t work out. For Birdie, the pair went over the story’s emotional notes for months. “Lidia brought a repertoire of references that became my references too,” she says.

Those references include works from Lucretia Martel, Ousmane Sembene’s Black Girl, and Djibril Diop Mambéty’s Touki Bouki. I tell her that her film’s juxtaposing the lives of two sisters, one of whom has a sexual experience, recalls Ian McEwan’s 2001 novel, Atonement, and its Oscar-winning adaptation by Joe Wright. To this, she exclaims, “Oh my God!” Apparently, one of her actresses had mentioned the same film to her the day before we speak. “I read the synopsis,” she says. “That’s a great reference.”

To get to Sundance, Odigie Paige’s team applied in August 2025 with an incomplete film. “It felt like a long shot,” she says, so she perceives her acceptance as an offshoot of the festival’s rectitude. “It speaks to the integrity of the process.” 

The good news from Sundance was delivered in November, which spurred a bit of frenzy. The film needed to be complete within a few weeks. In the end, it took what the director calls a “very stressful month” to get it ready for its premiere in January.

The Sundance Screening

As anyone can imagine, Odigie Paige was nervous at the first public screening of the film. But she had no reason to be. The film was well-received.

“The premiere was so much more rambunctious that I imagined,” she says obviously elated. “I think they fell in love with the characters.”

Indeed, the enthusiastic reception assures her that there is an audience for Birdie and her future work. “People get the film,” she tells me. “We are a global audience of cinephiles and we can appreciate things that are critical and thoughtful even if it’s not extremely genre like comedy or romance.”

In making her film, she says she wasn’t trying to pander. “I will never make a Nigerian film to be positioned for an American audience. My goal is specificity. But it is interesting that the more specific your story is, the more you cross to a large audience.”

While on the subject of her Sundance reception, she notes her happiness at seeing people from her home country at the festival. “It is cool to have a community of Nigerian people showing up for Lady, showing up for Birdie.”

To close the interview, I ask what an ideal Sundance outcome would be. She responds readily. “Funders find me,” she says. “Development execs find me. We need money to tell these stories well.”

And with that she laughs, a brief full-throated, delight-carrying laughter.

excerpt.rendered: Born in Nigeria, raised in the US, Praise Odigie Paige has led a life fit for the movies.

title.rendered: Why We No Longer See Nollywood Stars In Adverts

content.rendered:
There was always something quite enjoyable about seeing Genevieve Nnaji hold a Lux bar that wouldn’t last a week in an advert. Same with Osuofia (Nkem Owoh) advertising car batteries on TV. Because you knew his movie archetype, a stingy man, you knew that those batteries would probably last longer than car itself. That, at least, was part of the appeal.

Fame was maybe a bigger part of the appeal. But product ads in the early 2000s and late 90s did factor in Nollywood archetypes—and that sold us even more on the product they were advertising. It must have been easy deliverables for whoever was in charge of marketing.

These days, fewer ads on TV or online utilise Nollywood stars. Why is that?

I believe the answer is that a combination of factors have led to advertisers relying less and less on the star-power of the Nollywood actor.

Poverty Or the Eradication of the Middle Class

In the early 2000s, Nollywood stars represented a middle-class to aspire to and this seemed attainable. Your most popular actors lived in Surulere, drove 1990s’ era vehicles and you might have gone to boarding school with their kids. Heck, I slept in the late great Justus Esiri’s house a few nights myself as a nobody from Oshodi.

This means that there was a likelihood that a product being advertised by a Nollywood star was something they were also likely to use. Car batteries, malaria medication, soap bars. As the industry grew and expectations of stars either by the public or by an industry high on its own supply of hubris, Nollywood stars lost the air of relatability that made them perfect avatars for products the everyday person could be swayed to buy.

An actor might agree to be the face of a low-budget android phone brand—but it would be almost impossible to see that actor attend an event and take selfies with that brand. Instead, a need to declare their high status would likely have them take selfies with the latest iPhone pro max model. The class-gap between the viewer and the Nollywood star today is too wide for many products to bridge.

Authenticity Deficit

This is related to the above. And Nollywood stars are not entirely to blame, outside of sports betting apps, what mass consumable can they advertise that their audience would believe they actually consume on a regular basis? Also, in an age of increased media awareness, the utility of a star when it comes to pushing a non-luxury product is diminished compared to (seeming) real-life testimonials of the average Joe and Joanna. This isn’t just a Nollywood issue. No, I do not believe that aside from D’banj and his Koko garri, a celebrity ever used a product tied to their name (cough, cough, Infinix’s Davido branded phone).

Credibility Deficit

The ease with which Nollywood stars have been co-opted into advertisements for shady, suspicious and downright fraudulent products and services have robbed them of credibility. It hardly makes sense for fast-scaling operations to employ them unless those businesses are actually shady. Even as only a small number of Nollywood acts might have been involved in such practices, there is that thing they say about a few bad apples.

Who is A Nollywood Star Anyway?

As Nigerian cinema is caught in the doldrums post-pandemic, cable faces a global reset, and YouTube becomes the home to Nollywood content at scale, who is a Nollywood star? Is it Deyemi Okanlawon or Maurice Sam? Bam Bam, Uche Montana or Adesua Etomi?

Is it who was last in a cinema project or someone who’s led a Netflix-licensed or commissioned project? Is it the person in a YouTube movie with 22 million views and 100x more impressions across social media?

The inability to define the new standard for what makes a Nollywood star in the eyes of the public, and not the establishment and their fiefdoms mean that making a play for a Nollywood star is hardly worth the trouble for a brand seeking wide notice. Advertisers would rather avoid the headache of trying to figure a consensus on what constitutes a Nollywood star of palpable influence.

The Inflection Point

Wait. What do you mean Nollywood stars aren’t used anymore? That’s not true! There’s a custard advert with Toyin Abraham. Bimbo Ademoye has a thing with an alcohol brand (Flying Fish).  Fireboy had a deal with a phone manufacturer (Tecno). Carter Efe is doing something with a phone brand (Vivo). The dancing starlet from Big Brother represented a fintech (Kuda Bank) for a while and…

Exactly, the further you go, the fewer the movie stars, the more the “influencers”.  

Movie and TV stars used to be the sole window through which the audience experienced storytelling, found characters to love or hate or laugh at and impose certain types of identities on. But now, thanks to the internet, influencers have filled that role and may be better at it. They’re spontaneous, unguarded, and are a whole archetype by themselves. No movies needed, just tons of reels and shorts in which their archetype is reinforced for the audience to instantly associate with going forward.

Ademoye might have cut her teeth in the beginning with movies and TV series but she came into her current prominence by adopting her character from an Uduak Isong film and doubling down on it across skits on YouTube, Instagram, Facebook, and everywhere else.Movie stars being product banners was not preordained. It was just a consequence of their popularity and visibility—which product owners could capitalise on. That remains the case today. As a result, today’s movie star needs to pull double-duty as an active content engagement machine to have any utility. Nollywood stars who understand this will be fine. Others probably won’t be.

excerpt.rendered: The internet has upended a major revenue outlet for Nollywood celebrities.

title.rendered: African Producers Accelerator Opens 2026 Call For Filmmakers

content.rendered:
The African Producers Accelerator (APA) has opened applications for its 2026 programme, offering mid-career African producers an opportunity to strengthen their companies, refine their business strategies and expand their international reach. It is the second edition of the programme.

Alongside other requirements, eligible producers are expected to have produced one of these: a feature-length narrative film, a feature documentary, a TV hour documentary, a TV series which have screened at an international festival or was broadcast beyond its country of production.

Run by Big World Cinema, brainchild of South African producer Steven Markovitz, in partnership with the Bertha Foundation and the National Film and Video Foundation of South Africa, and in association with the Durban FilmMart Institute and Central Film School, the 12-week programme will run from May to the end of July 2026.

“The African film industry is at a pivotal moment,” says Big World Cinema. “Strong, sustainable production companies are essential to ensuring that bold African stories continue to reach global audiences. APA exists to help support them.”

Unlike traditional training labs with fixed curricula, the APA is designed as a tailor-made programme structured around each producer’s company, project slate and strategic goals. Participants will take part in weekly one-on-one online advisory sessions, curated masterclasses and targeted consultations with international industry specialists in areas such as world sales, intellectual property, business affairs, development and financing.

The programme will culminate in a five-day in-person lab in Cape Town, where producers will refine their company presentations and project slates before pitching to a panel of investors. Participants will then attend the Durban FilmMart, where tailored meetings with potential financiers, sales agents, festival programmers and distributors will be arranged.

Participation in the programme is free, and the costs of attending the Cape Town lab and Durban FilmMart will be covered.

The initiative targets African producers who have been working professionally for at least three years, run active production companies and have produced work that has screened internationally or been broadcast outside its country of origin.

The programme applications window opened today, 12 March 2026. It closes on 5 April 2026. Interested producers are required to fill this form. More information here.

excerpt.rendered: Second edition of the programme kicks off with a call for applications.

title.rendered: Lani Aisida: Are New YouTube Clips Diluting The Magic of “Dragons’ Den”?

content.rendered:
I’m an avid fan of Dragon’s Den. I watch it the same way I watch TV shows based on true events, like Narcos. How? Well, when watching Narcos, I’m constantly pausing to run to Google: Was Rodrigo Lara really assassinated? Was that really the Los Extraditables logo? Was Pablo Escobar really disgraced in Congress, and did he partner with M19 to burn down the Court?

I feed my Dragon’s Den addiction on YouTube, where each business pitch is uploaded as a standalone video, unlike the BBC One broadcast where multiple pitches make an episode. And after consuming a video, I dash to Google. I want to see how the pitched businesses are performing. Like Rob Law’s suitcase in 2006: told the company was worthless, it sold for £12 million in 2023. Did Sara Davies’ dad really get 5% of Redcoat Leisure? These nuggets fascinate me.

I’d estimate there have been about 1,000 pitches on Dragon’s Den since its inception in 2005, and I’ve watched about 800 of them. I wonder why I love it so much; maybe I just like business. But then, why am I not so into Shark Tank? Probably because those are “sharks”. Dragons are a bit more conservative in their ask, apart from that one time in 2011 when Duncan Bannatyne invested £59k for 79% equity in RKA Records, which was owned by teenagers. Some have argued that Bannatyne bought the company (which he later changed to Bannatyne Records) for his own entertainment. Maybe they are right: Despite several name changes, it has produced only one music video in its lifetime.

When Ultima Studios secured the rights to produce Lion’s Den, the Nigerian adaptation of Dragon’s Den, I knew I’d be one of the first to tune in. But aside from Adenike Ogunlesi, the “Lions” were new to me. So I did the “Narcos thing”. On Google, I found an account of how Paul Onwuanibe scoured Lagos in a helicopter to choose a space for Landmark beach. That was interesting.

Recently, I’ve also been following Oya! Pitch, a new format that feels inspired by the Dragon’s Den spirit. I’ve watched every episode, and I’m fascinated by how they’ve localised elements of the show. Instead of the standard “I’m out” you hear on Dragon’s Den, they use “This one pass me“.

Why Dragons’ Den works

But after watching some of the newly uploaded videos, I wasn’t feeling it. I had to stop and ask myself: what’s different? The format hasn’t changed, so what has? It made me go back to understand what made the previous episodes work so magnificently.

First, it’s emotional. From Levi Roots’ popular Reggae Reggae Sauce success story to Craig Hill’s tragic story, or the mom who had invested £250,000 of her own money in  her 15-year-old son’s Boot Buddy idea before they entered the den, these are touching stories.

It’s a business show, but it hits all the right notes without relying on cheap “sob stories”. Kirsty Henshaw’s episode, for example, resonated with me. She was authentic. I felt for her because she was just doing what she could with what she had. When Theo Paphitis said she was amazing and she sobbed, muttering “not really”, you could see the years of hustle behind those tears. Based on her comment on the YouTube video, she bought her shares back from Peter Jones and Duncan Bannatyne. She rebranded as Kirsty’s—I wonder if her boyfriend proposed to her—and it’s inspiring to know her company is now worth over £7 million.

I’m inspired more when I see Nigerian entrepreneurs in the Den. Whether it’s MKO Abiola’s daughter or Chika getting five offers for the snacks of my childhood, I feel some pride seeing our stories on the platform. Then there’s the episode with mother-son duo Sade and Matthew, a total rollercoaster. It starts with them in traditional outfits, singing a song I sang every morning in devotion as a child and a lot of “Nigerian mother” interactions that only Touker, himself from an immigrant family, could relate to. Even though it ended in tears (literally) and they didn’t get an investment, I loved them.

Secondly, it’s an entertaining crash course on entrepreneurship. There are decades of experience weighted in the questions the Dragons ask. You see confident entrepreneurs start to wobble when Deborah Meaden asks for the patent application or a specific contract. It’s intense and educative.

Thirdly, it’s entertaining. Perhaps, this should have been my first point. It’s high stakes and you can feel it through the screen. Like the Dragons, I guess what the pitch is when I see what’s on display and I’m eager to hear the pitch. The entrepreneur’s interrogation is like a game of ping-pong. Sometimes the Dragons bash an idea just to make others opt out, only to make an offer when they are the only ones left standing. It’s also interesting to see people go to the “wall” for advice. And British humour? It’s my favorite kind. Listening to Touker Suleyman say he doesn’t get out of bed for 1%, only to get the epic reply, “but you’re already out of bed”, from Helen Guillaume was brilliant television.

The “New” Den: What’s Different?

So, what is missing in the new episodes on YouTube? I noticed a few jarring changes:

  • The Cold Open: I miss the uncertainty of the elevator doors opening. I understand that YouTube algorithm demands a “hook” in the first five seconds to capture attention immediately, but it feels like there’s no foreplay anymore. Everyone just wants to get … you know what I mean. I guess it’s the world we live in now. Hollywood trailers are now cut to start with a cold open, usually a high action sequence for a few seconds before you see the intro text: “Trailer Starts Now”. Evolve or die, sadly.  
  • The Cue Cards: In a recent episode, Gulshen Bano reads her pitch off cue cards. Watching entrepreneurs stumble and recover is part of the Dragons’ Den thrill; seeing them read takes away the “high-stakes” feel. But maybe this is a one-off.
  • The Color Grading: The new episodes are much more colorful. But I prefer the dinginess of the earlier seasons; it added a layer of intensity. Now, the Den feels too welcoming.
  • The Length: I wonder how much entertainment value is sacrificed to keep the new episodes under 10 minutes on YouTube. Older episodes captured the exchange between the show’s personalities better. I rarely wondered how long entrepreneurs spend in the den. Now I do.
  • Guest Dragons: Normally when there’s a guest judge, we have six dragons. But now, it seems guest judges take the place of possibly my favorite dragon, Sara Davies. I assume the show’s producers have their reasons, but it changes the chemistry of the room. That said, I am not not a fan of guest judges.

I know that changes always happen. Even looking through past episodes, I see that the show always made subtle changes—like cutting out Evan Davis. So, even as I lament these changes on YouTube, Dragons’ Den remains a fave. It’s one of global TV’s most re-watchable formats.

***

Lani Aisida is a Nigerian screenwriter and producer who has worked on TV for over a decade

title.rendered: The Critics Awards for Africa to Recognise Excellence in Film and Television

content.rendered:
The Critics Awards for Africa is a new annual awards platform dedicated to recognising excellence in Nigerian/African film and television, with a deliberate emphasis on craft, artistry, ambition, and creative intention over popularity or box-office performance.

The inaugural Critics Awards for Africa will take place in the early weeks of the second quarter of 2026. Further details will be rolled out in the coming weeks.

Founded by Nigerian film critic Oris Aigbokhaevbolo, TCAA is positioned as a critics-led intervention within Nigeria’s fast-expanding screen industries. The awards are designed to foreground ambitious writing, directing, editing, sound and performance at a moment when African cinema is attracting unprecedented global visibility. Marketing and production for TCAA are handled mainly by One Management, led by entertainment executive Emem Ema.

The awards will feature about a dozen competitive categories across film and television, including Best Film, Best Series, Best Documentary, Best Writing for Screen, Best Directing, Best Editing, Best Sound, Best Performance, and Best Supporting Performance. To be eligible, films and shows would have to be released to the public between January and December 2025.

Nominees and winners will be selected by a jury composed predominantly of Nigerian critics, complemented by a smaller proportion of Western critics with sustained engagement with African and global cinema, alongside a limited number of experienced entertainment industry figures. This structure is intended to balance local critical authority with international perspective while maintaining independence. 

TCAA founder Oris Aigbokhaevbolo said: “African cinema, and Nigerian cinema in particular, is increasingly discussed in terms of business growth, scale, and visibility, which is welcome. But filmmaking is also an art, so we should pay attention to craft and artistic ambition: How our films are made, what they are trying to do, and how well they succeed. This critics’ awards project exists to centre excellence, artistry, intention and serious critical evaluation. We will begin with a Nigerian focus and take it from there.”

Aigbokhaevbolo is a Nigerian film critic and cultural writer whose work has appeared in The Washington Post, The Film Verdict, The Guardian, and Sight & Sound. He is the founder of filmefiko.com, an African cinema-focused publication, and is widely recognised for his sustained engagement with Nigerian and African film within global contexts.

Beyond the awards ceremony, TCAAThe Critics’ Awards for Africa plans to develop industry conversations, curated screenings and archival initiatives aimed at contextualising Nigerian film and television for both domestic and international audiences.

Submission guidelines and more eligibility criteria will be announced in due course.

title.rendered: Olasunkanmi Adebayo Talks Casting Challenges On “Lady”, Nigeria’s Sundance 2026 Project

content.rendered:
Olasunkanmi Adebayo or Suki, as he is fondly called, has developed several relationships in the Nigerian film and TV scene in the many years he has worked in it. One of those relationships is with Emporium Films, a production outfit he has collaborated with on TV commercials and film projects. So, he may have assumed it was another one of those projects he was to work on when, sometime in early 2023, he was contacted by Jamiu Soyode, one of Emporium’s producers.

But the project Soyode was calling about, a film titled Lady, was a bit unusual. The company was working with first-time feature director Olive Nwosu and she wanted to bring actors and actual sex workers together. Suki was interested; he had some experience in looking in what he calls “unconventional talent pools”. Sometime later he met Nwosu and they “aligned quickly on her vision and commitment to authenticity”.

The process of casting wasn’t as quick as their alignment. Indeed, by the time his work was complete, it was December 2024. This, he tells Film Efiko, is not how Nigerian productions work. “The biggest difference was time and intentionality,” he says. “Casting unfolded over 14 months, which allowed for deep exploration and due diligence. Given the emotional and physical demands of the film, we worked closely with psychologists and intimacy coordinators to prepare actors safely and responsibly.”

Casting Sex Workers

Naturally, there were challenges, chiefly because it was difficult to find sex workers who were willing to take part in a production that was partly about their lives. “The process required trust-building, sensitivity, and time,” Suki says. “We scouted extensively across Lagos and other southwestern states, searching for performers with the right emotional temperament and screen presence.”

To get it right, Suki and his team were involved in viewing what he says were “hundreds of self-tapes” as well as visiting theatre productions, churches, universities, and, yes, brothels. “Olive is a gentle taskmaster with a very intentional process,” he says. “So, we had scouting, training, workshops, screen tests, and character development before making final casting decisions.”

As it turned out, finding screen-ready sex workers was not the only tricky part of his job. Another was finding trained middle-aged actors, partly because there isn’t a centralised database for actors. “Finding actors in their 40s and 50s remains a particular challenge in Nollywood,” he says.

Casting Bucci Franklin

Then came the challenge of casting Bucci Franklin, perhaps the most recognisable actor in the film’s list of cast members. It “was a journey in itself,” he says.

Asked to explain, Suki says, Franklin is a “very specific kind of actor”. For some, this would mean he’s famous. Suki, however, means something quite different. “Olive and I needed someone who could hold quiet authority without overpowering the story.”

Franklin seemed to be the right fit. But there were logistical difficulties with getting Franklin. He was not in Lagos and he was booked and busy on other productions. In short, he was unable to send in a self-tape. The Lady team persisted and, somehow, was able to get through to the actor eventually. They flew him to Lagos from Port Harcourt for screen tests and in-person readings. “We needed to be absolutely sure the character chemistry, tone, and emotional restraint aligned with the world of the film.”

The crew’s patience paid off. “When it finally clicked, it felt inevitable,” Suki says now.

Beyond casting such a known name, other challenges included “sourcing a Chinese actor” and “casting children and actors with dwarfism”. “It became a carnival of casting,” says Suki.

Sundance and Berlinale Rewards

Nwosu was already in the Sundance pipeline, having shown a short at the festival years ago. So, perhaps Lady’s Sundance premiere was foretold. The film, however, has achieved something unprecedented for Nigerian coproductions at major festivals. It is the first Nigerian coproduction that has gotten invited to Sundance and the Berlin Film Festival in the same year. (It receives a European premiere at the Berlinale in February.) This level of international success, Suki believes, provides an opportunity for Nigerian actors.

“The producers and director took a bold step by backing a fully local cast in an international co-production space where recognisable global names are often prioritised,” he says. “Partners like HanWay Films, BFI, and Film4 supporting this approach opens real pathways for Nollywood actors to position themselves globally.”

It does feel like an important point to make, as Lady comes on the heels of My Father’s Shadow, the Nigerian co-production that was the country’s main international success story last year, given its premiere and reception at the Cannes film festival. Father’s Shadow was also backed by the BFI and featured the well-known British actor Sope Dirisu in the leading role. By contrast, Lady stars Jessica Gabriel’s Ujah, an actress who isn’t a household name in Nigeria.

As Suki explains, in seeking an actress to play lead, the crew came up with a list of performers whose quality of work isn’t matched by their popularity. “Jessica stood out immediately from her self-tape,” Suki says. “Even in that early submission, there was a stillness and emotional intelligence that felt rare.” She came even closer to snagging the role when she came in to perform for the team.

“Olive and I shortlisted her among our top three almost instantly,” he says. “When she steps into a scene, she transforms.”

Strong Production Structure

Besides the challenges of the casting process, Suki says Lady’s production structure was stellar. “We had a strong production backbone from detailed screen and camera tests to intensive location recces, scene breakdowns, and clearly articulated call sheets.”

All of which makes obviously Suki glad, especially as a player on the national scene, he believes there are lessons to be ferried into the average set across the country. “Not every production can operate at that scale,” he says, “but many of these processes are adaptable and invaluable even for smaller productions.”

Industry watchers will probably be looking to see if some of these practices do make it into mainstream Nollywood. For now, though, the main test of the utility of the structural novelties of this semi-Nigerian production is the quality of Lady itself. Has he seen it? What does he think of it?

“I found it bold and deeply moving,” he says. “From the opening moments, Alana Mejía González’s cinematography pulled me in.”

He then goes on to talk about the film’s sound design, music, and visual language as setting up the city of Lagos as “both beautiful and brutal. The audience isn’t allowed to look away: one moment you’re immersed in the underbelly of Lagos, the next you’re laughing, shocked.”

You are on the verge of setting down an entire review, I tell him.

He laughs and says, “But you asked”.

Lady premiered at the Sundance Film Festival on 22 January. It is available for screening for online festival guests.

excerpt.rendered: Casting director Olasunkanmi Adebayo (Suki) discusses his role on the set of Sundance-premiering feature “Lady”.

title.rendered: Africa Magic’s Split (Pilot) Review: Brilliant Premise, Hasty Execution

content.rendered:
To open 2026, the Africa Magic Showcase channel launched a new series based on a superb premise. Titled “Split”, it follows a group of struggling bank employees, Abdul, Harriet, and Tola, in Nigeria who come together to transfer money in a dormant account to their personal accounts. It’s an easy enough plan but its aftermath takes quite the toll on their lives. 

As with the bulk of Africa Magic stories, Split is relatable to the average Nigerian. Who hasn’t felt that a delay at the bank is caused by the shenanigans of staffers at the bank? This relatability, however, shouldn’t be a reason for the show’s cheap appearance and the story’s rushed narrative.

The picture could certainly look better and the story gentler told. The actors, Baaj Adebule and Annee Icha among them, deliver their roles well enough but the tone of the performances are sometimes uneven. This is especially the case with Baaj Adebule, who plays Abdul. He is the one who comes up with the idea of taking money lying fallow in an account and splitting it three ways. He also has a gambling problem. These details of his character make him out as quite interesting.

The trouble is he sometimes goes from comedic to serious, which is one source of the actor’s charm, but Split wants to have its cake and eat it too. Split wants charming Adebule to appear even when the scene doesn’t quite call for it. The character is evidently a ne’er-do-well, but he is also capable enough to rise within his bank. The tone of his performance in the pilot and the couple episodes released so far puts an emphasis on the former and not enough on the latter. Is this a funny character or a serious one who’s funny? The plot says one thing, the performance says another.

This instability in one of the show’s lead characters leads the show to feel like a sitcom instead of something sturdier in TV storytelling terms. The many interior scenes (usually indicative of a smaller budget) only add to the feeling that Split is a sitcom that missed its way.

It’s a disappointing state of affairs as this show could be as visually and narratively ambitious as Diiche, one of the premium Showmax Originals released in 2022. The premise of Split is certainly as deserving of the premium treatment as those first batch of shows on the streaming platform were. 

The producers (or perhaps commissioning team) seem to feel otherwise. And it’s a loss for viewers who would have been better entertained with a cooler, more sophisticated approach to a quite promising premise.

Split is currently showing on DSTV’s Africa Magic Showcase and on Showmax

excerpt.rendered: A quite remarkable premise is shortchanged with subpar execution in Africa Magic’s Split, a series about corporate theft gone wrong.

title.rendered: Fela & The Kalakuta Queens Review: Weak Writing Masked by Sex, Song, and Wonderful Stagecraft

content.rendered:
There’s a reason Fela Kuti has remained relevant, decades after his passing in 1997. His music is too infectious, his songwriting too strong, and his stage performances too erotically charged. 

The theatre and film director-producer Bolanle Austen-Peters seems aware of these qualities—enough that she deploys the relentless vigour of Fela’s music and style to bolster her own brilliant use of space, symmetry, and the body in this version of her most successful play, Fela And the Kalakuta Queens. She may also be aware to understand that the play’s weak writing and plotting can be ignored in the presence of Fela’s musical genius. 

What story there is really begins when Malaika, a lady who shows up, ostensibly seeking to study Fela, becomes enamoured of the maestro, turning the long-term women of the Fela household into canisters of jealousy. The relationship between these women and its fallout form the story’s main thread. Subplots emerge but they’re hardly treated seriously or satisfactorily.

These plots, if we can even call them that, are largely chapters from Fela and his women’s actual biographies wrapped around his popular songs but because they’re sloppily written, their only use is providing some distraction before the play dispenses another Fela hit. It becomes quite obvious that too little thought was given to how certain songs fit the story told. For instance, the narrative around “Lady” hardly works. The one for “Zombie” is tenuous. 

Feminist reading?

There is, of course, a feminist reclaiming of the women of Fela at play here. The women, after all, occupy somewhat equal billing with Fela in the title. But the weak playwriting prevents that from ever coming through strongly. Maybe the feminist angle works if the writing is strong as the music; it just isn’t. It’s not even close. Fela’s music is the strongest part of the play. How could it not be? In the near-three decades since his passing, Nigerian music isn’t over him.

Also, Fela is sui generis enough that it hardly seems possible that any entity in the real Kalakuta Republic—man, woman, or dog—could ever be on equal footing, titular prominence be damned. Which is one reason the play’s producers deserve plaudits for finding an excellent Fela. 

As Fela, ‘Laitan Adeniji, jazz player in his other life, commands the stage, his timbre, stature, and aura all forcing the case. He wears the late Kuti’s mannerism and peculiar outfits with aplomb. Is Adeniji our greatest Fela, a man with many copycats, even within his family? Well, he has my vote.

Staging sex appeal

His Queens are just as good. As with the Fela dancers of old, these Kalakuta Queens secrete a frenetic sexiness onstage. And the script puts a few sassy words in their mouth. In one scene, a record exec says, “This is a private property.” Comes the reply: “We don public am”. The delivery of that noun-verb flip is something. 

But the exceptional cast members can’t save the play’s latter half as the vigour with which the story begins ebbs. As it is with Austen-Peters’ film projects, the culprit is the writing: it’s much too weak to support the show’s lengthy runtime and the songs don’t show up frequently enough to distract the viewer from the malfunctioning narrative engine.
